title: Notes on building AI you can actually trust
summary: Essays and build notes on designing AI systems for regulated and high-complexity work, each anchored to a working tool, workflow, monitor, or operating layer.
audience: Leaders, practitioners, researchers, and builders evaluating AI for consequential work.

collection.heading: Start with the question that matches your work

evidence: Canonical research resources in the Aloha AI knowledge graph
Working tools and systems linked from each note
Dated primary and professional sources where claims require authority
methodology: Begin with a concrete system failure or design question
State the strongest competing account
Trace the mechanism behind the problem
Connect the reasoning to a bounded, inspectable build
assumptions: Readers distinguish systems commentary from professional advice
Linked tools and sources are inspected within their stated maturity and limits
limitations: The collection is not legal, tax, medical, or other professional advice
Research notes are maintained resources and may change as evidence, systems, and governing authority change

title: How I think about hallucination risk in legal and regulatory work
summary: Why fabricated citations are a predictable consequence of probabilistic text generation, which structural signals expose them, and why existence verification plus qualified human review matter more than waiting for a better model.
audience: Attorneys, legal-operations leaders, legal-technology teams, regulators, and builders of high-stakes research workflows.
evidence: Structural citation rules, reporter ranges, court and date constraints
Existence, proposition, pinpoint, and subsequent-history verification in authoritative legal sources
Applicable duties of competence, candor, supervision, and filing responsibility
methodology: Treat fluent citation output as an unverified candidate rather than authority
Run deterministic structural checks before paid or human research
Verify that the authority exists and supports the stated proposition
Check current treatment and require the responsible professional to approve consequential use
assumptions: Qualified professionals retain responsibility for legal judgment
Authoritative legal-research systems are available for existence and treatment checks
limitations: Structural validity cannot prove that a case exists or supports a proposition
This systems and evaluation research is not legal advice and creates no attorney-client relationship

title: What I audit first when a team says it is already using AI
summary: The six dimensions to inspect before selecting another tool: grounding, verification, data handling, human handoffs, policy alignment, and measurement.
audience: Organizations already using AI informally and leaders accountable for turning scattered adoption into a visible, governed practice.
evidence: Representative AI-assisted tasks and source materials
Approved-tool, retention, confidentiality, and data-handling records
Verification, approval, policy, training, incident, and performance records
methodology: Identify whether outputs are grounded in named sources
Inspect factual, numerical, and citation verification requirements
Map what data leaves organizational control and under which terms
Locate the human handoff and accountable owner
Compare written policy with observed practice
Measure quality, time, failures, overrides, and improvement
assumptions: The team permits inspection of representative real workflows and records
Leaders are willing to distinguish actual practice from aspirational policy
limitations: A maturity score is directional and does not establish legal or regulatory compliance
This systems and evaluation research is not legal advice

title: Tracking is not intelligence: designing a regulatory-analysis system
summary: Why comprehensive update feeds still leave decision-makers uninformed, and how issue taxonomy, comparison, sourcing, and audience-specific output turn collection into decision-ready intelligence.
audience: Regulatory, legal, strategy, and operating teams that must act on changing rules across jurisdictions or institutions.
evidence: Complete, dated primary-source records for each monitored change
Documented audience decisions, deadlines, and operational consequences
methodology: Define an audience-specific issue taxonomy before collection
Classify every update against decision-relevant categories
Compare signals across jurisdictions, time, and the organization's current posture
Trace every comparison to dated sources
Publish distinct outputs for counsel, operators, and boards
assumptions: Coverage is broad enough to support the comparisons being made
The decisions and audiences the system serves are explicitly defined
limitations: No monitoring system guarantees immediate detection of every change
Information and comparison support qualified decision-makers but do not replace legal or regulatory judgment

title: The difference between an AI tool, a workflow, and an operating system
summary: A practical distinction between a single capable act, a repeatable governed workflow, and the operating layer that orchestrates, evaluates, audits, and sustains many workflows across an organization.
audience: Executives, operators, legal and compliance leaders, and technology buyers deciding what kind of AI capability they actually need.
evidence: Defined inputs, output standards, verification gates, owners, and storage for each workflow
Cross-workflow policy, evaluation, audit, orchestration, and adoption records
Observed differences between individual tool use and reproducible institutional practice
methodology: Identify the single task a tool performs
Specify the inputs, standards, verification, human gate, and record that make the task repeatable
Add orchestration, evaluation, policy, audit, and adoption across workflows
Test whether the organization can reproduce and defend the resulting work
assumptions: Organizations can name accountable owners and preserve workflow records
Tool capability and institutional governance are evaluated as separate dimensions
limitations: The operating-system framing describes an organizational layer, not a claim that one software product governs every use
This systems and evaluation research is not professional advice

title: A legal AI workflow you can defend, not a chatbot you have to babysit
summary: A teardown of a legal research and drafting pipeline that locates hallucination risk, requires source and reporter checks, and keeps qualified human verification on the load-bearing decision.
audience: Law-firm partners, general counsel, eDiscovery counsel, legal-operations teams, and legal-AI buyers.
evidence: Reporter, proposition, pinpoint, and subsequent-history checks
Workflow logs showing inputs, generated work, verification, exceptions, and accountable approval
methodology: Define the legal task, jurisdiction, approved sources, and prohibited model roles
Retrieve candidate authority before drafting around it
Return an explicit null when controlling authority is not verified
Verify existence, proposition, pinpoint, and current treatment
Require the responsible professional to approve any filing, advice, or external work product
assumptions: A licensed attorney controls legal judgment, supervision, and final use
The workflow has authorized access to current legal-research sources
limitations: The illustrative fabricated citation is a demonstration rather than a real matter
Risk scoring and workflow design do not establish compliance or replace attorney research and judgment
